title: United 173 Runs Out of Fuel
text:
On the evening of 28 December 1978, United Airlines Flight 173, a DC-8 with 189 people on board, was approaching Portland, Oregon. When the crew lowered the landing gear there was a loud thump and one of the indicator lights did not show that the gear was down and locked.

Captain Malburn McBroom put the plane into a holding pattern to work the problem and prepare the cabin for a possible emergency landing. For about an hour the crew circled near the airport. During that time the flight engineer and the first officer each mentioned the fuel situation, but in hesitant terms, and the captain remained absorbed in the landing gear and the cabin preparations. Neither pressed him forcefully, and he did not act on what they said.

At about 6:06 p.m. the engines began to flame out from fuel exhaustion. The plane came down in a wooded suburban area several miles short of the runway. Ten people died, including the flight engineer, and many more were injured. The landing gear, it turned out, had been down all along.

The National Transportation Safety Board found that the probable cause was the captain's failure to monitor the fuel and to respond to the crew's advisories, and that the other crew members had failed to make their concern clear. It recommended training that would teach crews to work together and speak up. United responded by building one of the first crew resource management programs in the industry.
lesson: Hinting at a danger is not the same as raising it. If you see the team heading for trouble, say so plainly and make sure the leader has heard you.
people: Malburn McBroom and the crew of United Airlines Flight 173
source: National Transportation Safety Board, Aircraft Accident Report NTSB-AAR-79-7 (1979)
